screens.title: Feature-Based Project Structure
screens.narratorSegment: A deliberate folder structure is the single most effective simple habit for keeping an Unreal C++ project maintainable. Feature-based organization groups related C++ classes and assets under the same logical feature, for example Source/YourGame/Public/Characters and Source/YourGame/Private/Characters for code, and Content/Characters/Player or Content/Weapons/Rifle for assets. This reduces time spent searching for files and makes it clear which team owns a feature. Naming conventions matter: prefix actor classes with A, UObject-derived helper classes with U, enums with E, and structs with F. These prefixes are not decorative — they let developers understand a type at a glance and avoid confusion during code reviews. A common misconception is that flat folders are simpler; in practice, monolithic folders quickly become noisy and slow onboarding. A concrete example: if you add a new weapon type, create Weapon header and source files inside Source/YourGame/Public/Weapons and Source/YourGame/Private/Weapons and place its meshes and particle effects under Content/Weapons/Rifle. Key takeaway: consistent structure and naming speed development and reduce merge conflicts. Try this: pick one feature, reorganize its code and assets into feature folders, and note how quickly you can locate related files.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Feature-Based Project Structure
Definition

Organize by feature, not file type

Group C++ and assets around gameplay features so related code and art live close together and teams can work independently.

Recommended Source layout
Source/YourGame/Public/Characters Source/YourGame/Private/Characters Source/YourGame/Public/Weapons Source/YourGame/Private/Weapons
Recommended Content layout
Content/Characters/Player Content/Weapons/Rifle Content/UI/HUD
Common-mistake
Avoid dumping all code or assets in one folder; this increases friction and merge conflicts.
Key Takeaway

Feature-based folders and clear prefixes make project scale predictable and team-friendly.

Example
Content/
  Characters/
    Player/
      Meshes/
      Animations/
  Weapons/
    Rifle/
      Meshes/
      FX/
Source/YourGame/
  Public/
    Characters/
      MyPlayerCharacter.h (APlayerCharacter)
    Weapons/
      RifleWeapon.h (AWeapon)
  Private/
    Characters/
      MyPlayerCharacter.cpp
    Weapons/
      RifleWeapon.cpp
Why naming prefixes?
Prefixing classes (A, U, F, E) gives instant type context and prevents misuses like treating a struct as an Actor.

screens.title: What is a Plugin?
screens.narratorSegment: A plugin in Unreal Engine is a self-contained unit that can include C++ code, assets, editor tools, or runtime systems, packaged so it can be added or removed from different projects. Plugins compile to separate modules, typically containing their own Source/Public and Source/Private folders and a. Build. cs file that lists dependencies. You create them via the Editor's New Plugin wizard. Practical uses include reusable gameplay systems such as inventory or dialogue, third-party SDK integration, team separation where one team maintains a plugin and another uses it, and modding APIs that expose a clean surface for external creators. An everyday example: write a MyUtilityPlugin that exposes a UBlueprintFunctionLibrary with a GetGreetingMessage function; any project that includes the plugin can call that function without copying code. Common misconceptions: plugins are not only for editor extensions — runtime gameplay plugins are valid — and plugins are not free from maintenance costs; small one-off systems may add unnecessary overhead if split into plugins. Key decision rule: if you expect reuse across projects or want a clear public A P I, a plugin is beneficial; if the logic is tightly coupled to your game's unique features, keep it in the main game module.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › What is a Plugin?
Concept

Self-contained, shareable module

Plugins package code and assets, compile as a separate module, and expose a public API for other projects to use.

When to use a plugin
  • Reusable systems across projects (inventory, dialogue)
  • Third-party SDK encapsulation
  • Team separation and modding APIs
Common-mistake
Don't plugin-ize every small feature; small, game-specific code is simpler kept in the main module.
Key Takeaway

Plugins encapsulate and share functionality, but they add maintenance — choose them for reuse and clear API needs.

Quick Example: MyUtilityPlugin
// MyUtilityPlugin.Build.cs (excerpt)
using UnrealBuildTool;

public class MyUtilityPlugin : ModuleRules
{
  public MyUtilityPlugin(ReadOnlyTargetRules Target) : base(Target)
  {
    PCHUsage = ModuleRules.PCHUsageMode.UseExplicitOrSharedPCHs;

    PublicDependencyModuleNames.AddRange(
      new string[]
      {
        "Core",
        "CoreUObject",
        "Engine"
      }
    );
  }
}
Runtime check
After creating the plugin, add a UBlueprintFunctionLibrary class and a static function. Compile and call it from any Blueprint to verify the plugin loads correctly.

screens.title: Create a Blank Plugin & Configure .Build.cs
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a plugin is a small multi-step process that the Editor helps automate, but understanding what the wizard creates is essential. First, use Edit → Plugins → New Plugin and choose Blank. The wizard generates a plugin folder with a Descriptor file, a Resources folder for icons, and a Source folder containing Public and Private directories. The plugin's. Build. cs file defines how the module is compiled and declares dependencies. Add CoreUObject and Engine to PublicDependencyModuleNames when your plugin needs engine types or UObject features. A concrete step: open Source/MyUtilityPlugin/MyUtilityPlugin. Build. cs and ensure it lists Core, CoreUObject and Engine in PublicDependencyModuleNames. AddRange. Then add a new C++ class inside the plugin, for example a UBlueprintFunctionLibrary-derived class with a static function GetGreetingMessage that returns "Hello from MyUtilityPlugin!". Restart the editor when the wizard requests it, compile, then test the function in a Blueprint. A common mistake is adding engine dependencies in the wrong list — public vs private — which can change the visibility of headers; keep core runtime dependencies in PublicDependencyModuleNames if other modules will include your headers. Final check: the plugin compiles cleanly and exposes the expected Blueprint node.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Create a Blank Plugin & Configure .Build.cs
Step-by-step
  1. Create: Edit → Plugins → New Plugin → Blank, give it a name like MyUtilityPlugin.
  2. Restart the Editor when prompted so the plugin registers with the build system.
  3. Inspect the generated folder: MyUtilityPlugin/Source/MyUtilityPlugin/Public and /Private.
  4. Edit MyUtilityPlugin.Build.cs to add dependencies and set PCH usage.
  5. Add a UBlueprintFunctionLibrary class inside the plugin, implement a test function, compile and call it from Blueprint.
Check

Plugin compiles and the Blueprint node appears — success.

Code example
// MyUtilityPlugin.Build.cs
using UnrealBuildTool;

public class MyUtilityPlugin : ModuleRules
{
  public MyUtilityPlugin(ReadOnlyTargetRules Target) : base(Target)
  {
    PCHUsage = ModuleRules.PCHUsageMode.UseExplicitOrSharedPCHs;

    PublicDependencyModuleNames.AddRange(
      new string[]
      {
        "Core",
        "CoreUObject", // Add this
        "Engine"       // Add this
      }
    );
  }
}
Tip
Put headers you want other modules to include in the plugin's Public folder. Use Private for internal implementation files.

screens.title: Implement a Simple Utility Class in a Plugin
screens.narratorSegment: After configuring your plugin's build settings, the next step is to add a concrete class that proves the pipeline works. A common and simple choice is a UBlueprintFunctionLibrary class because its static methods are callable from Blueprints without instancing. Create UMyBlueprintFunctionLibrary inside Source/MyUtilityPlugin/Public and implement a static function GetGreetingMessage that returns a plain FString like "Hello from MyUtilityPlugin!". Place implementation in the Private folder and add proper module export macros if necessary. Compile the project, then open the editor, create or open a Blueprint, and search for the node named Get Greeting Message to confirm the function is exposed. A concrete code example is shown in the code panel. One subtle pitfall: forgetting to add CoreUObject or Engine to PublicDependencyModuleNames can cause missing types at compile time. Another is placing header files in Private — those headers won't be visible to other modules or Blueprint, so public A P I must be in Public. Once the function appears in Blueprint and returns the expected string, you have a minimal working plugin. Ask yourself: could this functionality be useful across projects? If yes, it's a keeper; if it's only game-specific, prefer the main module.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Implement a Simple Utility Class
Header (Public)
// MyUtility.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "Kismet/BlueprintFunctionLibrary.h"
#include "MyUtility.generated.h"

UCLASS()
class UMyUtility : public UBlueprintFunctionLibrary
{
  GENERATED_BODY()

public:
  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "MyUtility")
  static FString GetGreetingMessage();
};
Implementation (Private)
// MyUtility.cpp
#include "MyUtility.h"

FString UMyUtility::GetGreetingMessage()
{
  return FString(TEXT("Hello from MyUtilityPlugin!"));
}
Verification Steps
  • Compile the project and restart the editor if required.
  • Open a Blueprint, right-click, and search for "Get Greeting Message".
  • Call the node and print the returned string to the screen or log.
Common-mistake
Placing public API headers in Private prevents other modules or Blueprint from seeing them.
Key Takeaway

A working blueprint-callable function proves plugin compilation and visibility; design Public headers as the plugin API.

screens.title: C++ Interfaces: A Contract for Modularity
screens.narratorSegment: An interface is a formal contract that says: “any class implementing this interface must provide these functions.” In Unreal C++ this is expressed using UINTERFACE and an I-prefixed interface class. Interfaces let systems talk to each other without knowing concrete types. For example, if the player can interact with doors, pickups or NPCs, you don’t want the player to depend on ADoor or APickup classes. Instead, create an IInteractable contract that defines Interact. Any actor can implement it. This reduces compile-time dependencies and makes it easy to add new interactables later. A common misconception is to treat interfaces like multiple inheritance for implementation; they are contracts, not full behavior carriers. Use BlueprintNativeEvent when you want a C++ default implementation that Blueprints can override, or use pure virtual signatures if implementation must be provided by each class. As a concrete example, defining IInteractable and calling Implements () allows your player code to accept any object that claims the contract and call IInteractable::Execute_Interact to invoke the behavior. That single pattern improves testability, supports plugins, and prevents the player module from growing tight class dependencies. Think of interfaces as a handshake: the caller knows the promise, not the internals. How could your current systems benefit from that promise?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › C++ Interfaces
What it is

Interface contract

An interface declares functions a class must expose. It avoids knowing concrete implementations and reduces coupling between systems.

  • Defines a promise: method names and signatures.
  • Implemented by Actors or UObject-derived classes.
  • Supports BlueprintNativeEvent for optional C++ defaults.
Example use
Use IInteractable to let a single player interaction code work with doors, pickups, and NPCs without type checks.
Key Takeaway

Prefer interfaces when multiple unrelated classes need the same capability; prefer inheritance for shared implementation.

Code Example

IInteractable header & default impl

<!-- IInteractable.h -->
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "UObject/Interface.h"
#include "Interactable.generated.h"

UINTERFACE(MinimalAPI, Blueprintable)
class UInteractable : public UInterface
{
    GENERATED_BODY()
};

class YOURGAME_API IInteractable
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, BlueprintNativeEvent, Category = "Interaction")
    void Interact(AActor* Caller);
};


<!-- IInteractable.cpp -->
#include "Interactable.h"

void IInteractable::Interact_Implementation(AActor* Caller)
{
    // Optional C++ default behavior
    UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Default Interact called by %s"), *Caller->GetName());
}
Concrete example
A door implements IInteractable and overrides Interact_Implementation to play an animation and change open state. The player code never needs to know it is a door class.
Common mistake
Treating interfaces like multiple inheritance for shared data. Interfaces carry no member state; keep implementation separate.

screens.title: Implementing IInteractable in an Actor
screens.narratorSegment: Let's implement IInteractable in a concrete Actor so you can see the pattern in practice. First, add public IInteractable to your actor's header and declare Interact_Implementation. The I-prefixed interface requires the BlueprintNativeEvent signature in the header, but your implementing class overrides Interact_Implementation. In the door example, the override toggles an open boolean, plays a sound, and logs the interaction. This gives you predictable behavior for both C++ and Blueprint implementers. A frequent beginner error is to implement Interact instead of Interact_Implementation, which will not be called when using Execute_Interact. Another gotcha is forgetting GENERATED_BODY() placement in both the UINTERFACE and the interface class; compilation will fail silently if that macro is misplaced. After implementing the function, test in the editor by placing the actor and invoking the interface from a Blueprint or a simple player trace. If you use BlueprintNativeEvent, your Blueprint subclass can optionally override the Blueprint version to add visual polish while preserving a C++ fallback. This approach keeps the door's contract explicit, supports plugin reuse, and avoids coupling player logic to a specific door class. What default behavior would you include in a base implementation versus leaving for game-specific subclasses?

In the door example, the override toggles an open boolean, plays a sound, and logs the interaction. This gives you predictable behavior for both C++ and Blueprint implementers. A frequent beginner error is to implement Interact instead of Interact_Implementation, which will not be called when using Execute_Interact. Another gotcha is forgetting GENERATED_BODY() placement in both the UINTERFACE and the interface class; compilation will fail silently if that macro is misplaced. After implementing the function, test in the editor by placing the actor and invoking the interface from a Blueprint or a simple player trace. If you use BlueprintNativeEvent, your Blueprint subclass can optionally override the Blueprint version to add visual polish while preserving a C++ fallback. This approach keeps the door's contract explicit, supports plugin reuse, and avoids coupling player logic to a specific door class. Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Implement IInteractable
Header & override
// MyDoor.h
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "GameFramework/Actor.h"
#include "Interactable.h" // interface header
#include "MyDoor.generated.h"

UCLASS()
class AMyDoor : public AActor, public IInteractable
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    AMyDoor();

    virtual void Interact_Implementation(AActor* Caller) override;

private:
    bool bIsOpen = false;
};
CPP: toggle state & feedback
// MyDoor.cpp
#include "MyDoor.h"
#include "Kismet/GameplayStatics.h"

void AMyDoor::Interact_Implementation(AActor* Caller)
{
    bIsOpen = !bIsOpen;
    if (bIsOpen)
    {
        UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("Door opened by %s"), *Caller->GetName());
        // Play open animation or sound
    }
    else
    {
        UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("Door closed by %s"), *Caller->GetName());
    }
}
Testing scenario

Place AMyDoor in the level. From a player trace or Blueprint, detect the hit actor and call IInteractable::Execute_Interact(HitActor, Player). Confirm logs and animation play. If nothing happens, ensure the actor implements the interface and you used Execute_Interact rather than a direct cast.

Pro tip
Keep interaction side effects minimal inside the interface implementation. Use the interface to trigger a higher-level method that orchestrates animation, state, and audio separately for testability.
Key Takeaway

Implement Interact_Implementation in your actor classes and test via Execute_Interact to preserve the contract across C++ and Blueprints.

screens.title: Player-side: Detecting and Calling Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: The common runtime flow for interaction is: detect an object, verify it implements the interface, then call the contract method. A robust pattern uses a line trace or overlap to get a hit actor, then checks if it Implements the interface using Implements (). If true, call IInteractable::Execute_Interact(HitActor, ThisPlayer). This avoids casts to concrete classes and works for both C++ and Blueprint-implemented interactables. An important concrete example: on input, perform a short line trace from the camera; if you hit an actor, first check Valid and not the player, then if (HitActor->Implements ()) call Execute_Interact. A common mistake is casting to the UInterface type directly or calling the interface C++ function without using Execute_. That can fail when the object is a Blueprint implementation because the Blueprint thunk is hooked into the Execute_ wrapper. Also be careful with null Owner or mismatched Player pointer; log useful context during testing. Finally, think about permission checks: the interface can accept a Caller argument so the implementer can decide if that caller is allowed to interact. This preserves game rules inside the object rather than scattering them into the player code. Try the flow in editor and ask: where should permission checks live, caller or callee?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Player Interaction Flow
Code Pattern

Trace → Check → Execute

// PlayerCharacter.cpp (interaction snippet)
FHitResult Hit;
FVector Start = Camera->GetComponentLocation();
FVector End = Start + (Camera->GetForwardVector() * 500.0f);
FCollisionQueryParams Params;
Params.AddIgnoredActor(this);

if (GetWorld()->LineTraceSingleByChannel(Hit, Start, End, ECC_Visibility, Params))
{
    AActor* HitActor = Hit.GetActor();
    if (HitActor && HitActor->Implements())
    {
        IInteractable::Execute_Interact(HitActor, this);
    }
}
Why Use Implements()
It checks the object claims the contract, safe across Blueprint/C++ combinations and avoids fragile casts.
Common bug
Calling the interface method directly instead of Execute_ may bypass Blueprint overrides and crash or do nothing.
Scenario
On press of Interact, perform trace. If HitActor implements IInteractable, call Execute_Interact. Let objects validate callers internally for permissions.
Debug checklist
  • Is HitActor non-null and not the player?
  • Does it Implements()?
  • Did you call Execute_Interact rather than direct function?
  • Are Blueprint overrides present and compiled?
Key Takeaway

Use the trace-check-execute pattern so player code remains agnostic of interactable implementations and compatible with Blueprints.

screens.title: Plugin vs Game Module: Which to Use?
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding where to place code is critical for maintainability. Plugins are separate modules compiled independently and are ideal for reusable systems, third-party integrations, tools, or anything you might share across projects. Put a generic inventory, analytics, or editor tool in a plugin so it can be dropped into another project. Keep game-specific systems—scripting closely tied to design, single-use levels, or tightly-coupled gameplay logic—inside the game module. Overusing plugins for tiny features adds overhead and complicates builds; conversely, stuffing reusable systems into the game module makes them hard to extract later. Team structure matters: if separate teams own different features, plugins help enforce boundaries. For mod support, plugins provide a clear A P I surface for modders. A typical evaluation checklist looks at reusability, coupling, frequency of change, and ownership. Ask: will this feature be used by multiple projects? Will it be maintained by an independent team? If yes, prefer a plugin. If the answer is no, keep it in the game module to reduce complexity. A common mistake is moving code into a plugin too early; create a plugin when you have a working, reusable system to avoid refactoring churn. Ultimately, balance and pragmatism win: favor clarity of ownership and an architecture that supports long-term growth.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Plugin vs Game Module
Use a Plugin
  • Reusable across projects: inventory, dialogue, analytics.
  • Third-party SDKs: isolate integration and build deps.
  • Team separation: different teams work independently.
  • Modding surface: clear API for external authors.
Folder shape: Plugins/MyPlugin/Source/MyPlugin/Public and /Private, with a MyPlugin.Build.cs declaring Core, CoreUObject, Engine dependencies.
Keep in Game Module
  • Game-specific features: level-driven logic, single-use scripts.
  • Small utilities: trivial helpers that won't be reused.
  • Rapid iteration: faster to change without plugin rebuild cycles.
Folder shape: Source/YourGame/Public & /Private; Content features grouped under Content/FeatureName.
Scenario
A generic inventory system used across titles → plugin. A quest flow unique to a single game → game module.
Pitfall
Creating a plugin for a tiny, tightly-coupled feature increases build and maintenance overhead.
Key Takeaway

Favor clarity: use plugins for reusable, shared, or team-isolated systems; keep highly-specific, rapidly-changing code in the game module.

screens.title: Naming, Folder Layout & Team Guidelines
screens.narratorSegment: Consistent naming and folder layout save time as projects scale. Use Unreal’s common prefixes: A for Actors, U for UObject-derived types and Components, F for Structs, and E for Enums. Group C++ files under Source/YourGame/Public and Source/YourGame/Private, subdivided by feature like Characters, Weapons, UI, AI. Mirror that organization inside Content so artists and programmers find related assets together. For plugins, follow Plugins/PluginName/Source/PluginName/{Public,Private}. Keep public headers minimal and expose only what other modules need. In. Build. cs list only the dependencies required; avoid adding broad dependencies to prevent coupling. From a team perspective, define ownership: which team owns AI code, which owns UI, and set merge boundaries. Use code reviews to enforce naming rules and folder placement. Common mistakes include dumping unrelated classes into a single folder and inconsistent prefixes that slow onboarding. Also avoid placing small, game-specific helpers in shared plugin modules. Practical action: establish a short README at project root that documents folder rules, class prefixes, and plugin responsibilities. This small discipline reduces friction for new hires and simplifies refactors later. Which project area would benefit most from a cleanup in your codebase?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build an intuitive mental model for organizing Unreal Engine C++ projects so your codebase stays maintainable as it grows. You will learn a recommended folder layout for C++ and Content, why naming prefixes like A, U, E and F matter, and where to place game-specific logic versus reusable modules. We'll also introduce plugins as self-contained modules you can share across projects and teams, and explain C++ Interfaces — the contract pattern Unreal uses to let different systems interact without tight coupling. A short, concrete example you'll practice: create an IInteractable interface and a small utility plugin that provides a single blueprint-callable function. That exercise ties these ideas together: a clear project layout helps onboard teammates; plugins encapsulate reusable subsystems; interfaces let gameplay code call into many object types through a single contract. Watch for two common mistakes: stuffing everything into the main game module, and creating plugins for one-off, highly specific game logic. By the end you should understand how to decide when to keep code in the game module and when to split it into a plugin, and how interfaces reduce interdependency between systems.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to design a reproducible project layout, create and configure a simple plugin, implement a C++ interface, and make an informed decision about when to use a plugin versus placing code directly in your game module. First, you will establish effective folder structures and naming conventions so that your C++ classes and Content assets are grouped by feature and immediately understandable. Second, you will understand what a plugin is and the scenarios where plugins provide real benefit: reuse across projects, third-party SDKs, team separation, and modding support. Third, you will develop a basic custom plugin: create the plugin with the editor, inspect the generated Source/Public and Source/Private folders, and edit the plugin's. Build. cs to add CoreUObject and Engine dependencies. Fourth, you will implement a C++ interface using UINTERFACE and I[InterfaceName] macros, write a default implementation, and call it with Implements<> and Execute_. Each objective includes a short, practical milestone so you can verify competency: a folder layout review, a compiled plugin that exposes one blueprint-callable function, an implemented IInteractable actor, and a short justification for plugin vs project placement.

This continuation of objectives emphasizes practical verification and reinforces how you will apply these patterns in real code. You will practice creating an IInteractable interface step by step, add a default Interact implementation for BlueprintNativeEvent, and implement that interface on an AActor subclass such as a door. You'll test interaction by calling IInteractable::Execute_Interact from player code after a line trace. Another objective is to package a small utility plugin, add a UBlueprintFunctionLibrary class, and implement a simple function that returns a greeting string. Compiling and calling the function in a Blueprint proves the plugin pipeline. Finally, you will learn to evaluate placement decisions: keep small, game-specific code in the main module; choose plugins when a system is generic, reusable, or needs to be shared between projects or teams. Each objective includes a short milestone so you can mark competency: running a trace that triggers Interact, seeing the plugin function in Blueprint, and writing a concise justification for your architectural choice.

A deliberate folder structure is the single most effective simple habit for keeping an Unreal C++ project maintainable. Feature-based organization groups related C++ classes and assets under the same logical feature, for example Source/YourGame/Public/Characters and Source/YourGame/Private/Characters for code, and Content/Characters/Player or Content/Weapons/Rifle for assets. This reduces time spent searching for files and makes it clear which team owns a feature. Naming conventions matter: prefix actor classes with A, UObject-derived helper classes with U, enums with E, and structs with F. These prefixes are not decorative — they let developers understand a type at a glance and avoid confusion during code reviews. A common misconception is that flat folders are simpler; in practice, monolithic folders quickly become noisy and slow onboarding. A concrete example: if you add a new weapon type, create Weapon header and source files inside Source/YourGame/Public/Weapons and Source/YourGame/Private/Weapons and place its meshes and particle effects under Content/Weapons/Rifle. Key takeaway: consistent structure and naming speed development and reduce merge conflicts. Try this: pick one feature, reorganize its code and assets into feature folders, and note how quickly you can locate related files.

A plugin in Unreal Engine is a self-contained unit that can include C++ code, assets, editor tools, or runtime systems, packaged so it can be added or removed from different projects. Plugins compile to separate modules, typically containing their own Source/Public and Source/Private folders and a. Build. cs file that lists dependencies. You create them via the Editor's New Plugin wizard. Practical uses include reusable gameplay systems such as inventory or dialogue, third-party SDK integration, team separation where one team maintains a plugin and another uses it, and modding APIs that expose a clean surface for external creators. An everyday example: write a MyUtilityPlugin that exposes a UBlueprintFunctionLibrary with a GetGreetingMessage function; any project that includes the plugin can call that function without copying code. Common misconceptions: plugins are not only for editor extensions — runtime gameplay plugins are valid — and plugins are not free from maintenance costs; small one-off systems may add unnecessary overhead if split into plugins. Key decision rule: if you expect reuse across projects or want a clear public A P I, a plugin is beneficial; if the logic is tightly coupled to your game's unique features, keep it in the main game module.

Creating a plugin is a small multi-step process that the Editor helps automate, but understanding what the wizard creates is essential. First, use Edit → Plugins → New Plugin and choose Blank. The wizard generates a plugin folder with a Descriptor file, a Resources folder for icons, and a Source folder containing Public and Private directories. The plugin's. Build. cs file defines how the module is compiled and declares dependencies. Add CoreUObject and Engine to PublicDependencyModuleNames when your plugin needs engine types or UObject features. A concrete step: open Source/MyUtilityPlugin/MyUtilityPlugin. Build. cs and ensure it lists Core, CoreUObject and Engine in PublicDependencyModuleNames. AddRange. Then add a new C++ class inside the plugin, for example a UBlueprintFunctionLibrary-derived class with a static function GetGreetingMessage that returns "Hello from MyUtilityPlugin!". Restart the editor when the wizard requests it, compile, then test the function in a Blueprint. A common mistake is adding engine dependencies in the wrong list — public vs private — which can change the visibility of headers; keep core runtime dependencies in PublicDependencyModuleNames if other modules will include your headers. Final check: the plugin compiles cleanly and exposes the expected Blueprint node.

After configuring your plugin's build settings, the next step is to add a concrete class that proves the pipeline works. A common and simple choice is a UBlueprintFunctionLibrary class because its static methods are callable from Blueprints without instancing. Compile the project, then open the editor, create or open a Blueprint, and search for the node named Get Greeting Message to confirm the function is exposed. A concrete code example is shown in the code panel. One subtle pitfall: forgetting to add CoreUObject or Engine to PublicDependencyModuleNames can cause missing types at compile time. Another is placing header files in Private — those headers won't be visible to other modules or Blueprint, so public A P I must be in Public. Once the function appears in Blueprint and returns the expected string, you have a minimal working plugin. Ask yourself: could this functionality be useful across projects? If yes, it's a keeper; if it's only game-specific, prefer the main module.

An interface is a formal contract that says: “any class implementing this interface must provide these functions.” In Unreal C++ this is expressed using UINTERFACE and an I-prefixed interface class.
